title: From Horeb to Kadesh, Once More
sum: On the plains of Moab, in the fortieth year, Moses begins to "make this law clear" (1:5). He starts with memory. At Horeb God told Israel to set out for the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (1:6–8). Moses, unable to carry the people alone, had them choose wise leaders and judges, and charged them to judge fairly, small and great alike (1:9–18). At Kadesh the people asked to send scouts, heard their good report and their fears, and refused to go up (1:19–33). God swore that none of that generation but Caleb and Joshua would see the land. A late attack without God ended in defeat (1:34–46).

The chapter sets the tone of the whole book. The listeners are the children of the generation that failed, and Moses tells them their parents' story as a warning: the same choice now stands in front of them.
readings: Read as a sermon

Moses is not giving a neutral history. He chooses and arranges events to move his hearers: the generation at Kadesh had every reason to trust (God carried them "the way a man carries his son," 1:31), and still refused. The past is preached so that the present generation will choose differently. The repeated "you" merges the parents with the children, as if those listening had stood at Kadesh themselves.
Read beside Numbers

The same events are told in Exodus 18 and Numbers 13–14, and the differences are clear. In Numbers the LORD commands the scouting (Numbers 13:1–2); here the people propose it (1:22). In Exodus the idea of judges comes from Jethro; here Moses tells it without him. In Numbers Moses is barred from the land for what happened at Meribah (Numbers 20:12); here God is angry with Moses "because of you" (1:37). Traditional readers fit the accounts together; critical readers see separate traditions.

views.H: Moses speaks on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year (1:3), weeks before his death. He reviews events he lived through, and fills in details the earlier books leave out, such as the people's request for scouts. The two accounts complement each other: the people asked, Moses agreed, and God allowed it.
views.C: Chapters 1–3 are often read as the opening of the Deuteronomistic History, which Martin Noth held was written in the exile as a preface to Joshua through Kings. The retelling draws on the older stories behind Numbers 13–14 and Exodus 18 (non-priestly material) but not on the priestly parts, which suggests Deuteronomy's writers knew an earlier form of the Torah's stories.
views.T: Treaties from the Hittite empire open with a preamble naming the great king and a historical prologue of what he has done for his vassal. Deuteronomy 1:1–5 and 1:6–3:29 play these roles: the speaker, the setting, and a review of the LORD's past kindness and the people's past unfaithfulness, the grounds for the covenant that follows.
views.J: The rabbis read 1:1 as a hidden rebuke. They take its place names (Paran, Laban, Hazeroth, Di-zahab) as hints of Israel's sins: the scouts, the manna complaint, Korah, the golden calf (Sifre Deuteronomy 1; Rashi). Moses rebuked Israel only near his death, they say, so as not to shame them repeatedly. In the yearly cycle the portion Devarim falls on the Sabbath before the fast of the Ninth of Av, which mourns the temple's fall, and so the word eikhah, "How," in 1:12 is chanted to the tune of Lamentations, which begins with the same word.
views.X: Hebrews 3:7–4:11 reads the refusal at Kadesh, and the oath that the generation "will not enter my rest," as a warning to Christians not to harden their hearts. The charge to the judges, "do not play favorites," echoes in James 2:1–9.

deep.h: Who barred Moses from the land?
deep.b:
Deuteronomy says three times that God was angry with Moses "because of you" (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). It sets this inside the story of the scouts, thirty-eight years before Moses' death. Numbers instead ties it to Moses and Aaron at the waters of Meribah: "You did not believe me, to treat me as holy in the Israelites' eyes" (Numbers 20:12). Deuteronomy later knows that version too (see 32:51).

Readers explain this in several ways. Some, such as Ibn Ezra, take 1:37 as a flash-forward: Moses breaks into the Kadesh story to mention his own later punishment, because both happened "because of" the people's complaints at Kadesh. Others say Moses suffered as the leader of a guilty people, sharing their fate, a theme some Christian readers link to the suffering servant of Isaiah 53. Many critical scholars see two different explanations from different traditions: one in which Moses sins, and one in which he bears the people's guilt.

In Exodus 18 Jethro suggests that Moses appoint leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and Moses chooses them himself. In Deuteronomy Moses proposes it, the people choose "men who are wise, who have understanding and who are known" (1:13) from their tribes, and Moses appoints them (1:13–15). Traditional readers combine the two: Jethro gave the advice and Moses took it up as his own. Critical scholars often see in 1:16–17 the ideals of later Judean courts, such as the reform of King Jehoshaphat, who also told his judges that they judged for the LORD (2 Chronicles 19:5–7). The charge itself, not to favor the powerful and not to fear anyone, "because the judgment is God's" (1:17), became a basic text of Jewish law on judges (Bavli Sanhedrin 6b–8a).

deep.title: Claude's reading: 'because of you' as a preacher's move
deep.b: My own suggestion: Moses' words "because of you" (1:37; 3:26; 4:21) are part of the sermon's design, not only a different tradition. Moses ties his own fate to the people's unbelief so that his coming death on the wrong side of the Jordan becomes a living sermon to them. Every time they see him barred, they are to remember what unbelief costs. This does not settle the historical question of two traditions. It explains why Deuteronomy chooses this version for its opening chapters, while it keeps the Meribah version for the end of the book.

echoes: Genesis 15:5; Genesis 15:18; Exodus 18:13–26; Numbers 10:11–12; Numbers 11:14–17; Numbers 13:1–33; Numbers 14:1–45; Numbers 20:12; Joshua 14:6–14; 2 Chronicles 19:5–7; Psalm 95:7–11; Hebrews 3:7–4:11; James 2:1–9

settings.what: Moses' first speech: the road from Horeb
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year, after the defeat of Sihon and Og (1:3–5)
settings.why: Moses retells the journey from Horeb to the Jordan so that the new generation will not repeat their parents' refusal at Kadesh. He tells the old story as "you" and "us," as if his hearers had been there. Their parents' failure becomes their own warning. The history ends in a sermon on the one God who was heard but not seen (4:1–40). Read this way, the past is not a record but a choice that stands again in front of the hearers.
views: Traditional readers take the speech as Moses' own words to the people about to cross the Jordan.

Noth and many after him see 1:1–4:40 as written later, as the opening of the history that runs through Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings. Its readers were Judah in Josiah's day or the exiles. They would read the whole story of the land in its light.

settings.what: Moses recalls his charge to the judges
settings.by: Moses, recalling his words at Horeb
settings.to: All Israel at Horeb, who chose the leaders (1:13); then the judges Moses appointed (1:16–17); all recalled before all Israel on the plains of Moab
settings.why: Moses could not carry the people alone, so he shared the work with wise men over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. He charged the judges to hear small and great alike, and the foreigner too. They must fear no one, because the judgment is God's. Cases too hard for them came to him. Told again to the new generation, it shows that fair courts belong to the covenant from its start, and it prepares for the laws on judges in 16:18–17:13.

title: Lands Not Given, and a Land Given
sum: After the long years around Mount Seir, God tells Israel to turn north (2:1–3). They are to pass by the descendants of Esau in Edom, of Lot in Moab and Ammon, and pay for food and water, because God has given these peoples their lands as he will give Israel its own (2:4–23). Asides tell of older giant peoples whom God drove out for them. By the brook Zered the whole generation of fighting men has died (2:14–16). Then Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, refuses Israel passage. God makes his heart stubborn, and Israel defeats him and puts his towns under the ban (2:24–37).
The chapter's surprise is God's care for other nations. The LORD who gives Israel its land has also given Edom, Moab and Ammon theirs.
readings: Read as a map of God's gifts

The chapter is a lesson in boundaries. Three times God says "I will not give you any of their land" (2:5; 2:9; 2:19), because he has given it to others. Israel's claim to Canaan rests on gift, not on strength, and the same God rules the whole map. The ancient peoples who once lived in those lands, the Emim, the Zamzummim, the Horites and the Avvim, show that God has moved nations before (2:10–12; 2:20–23).
Read as the start of the conquest

At the Arnon the tone turns. "Begin to take possession" (2:24, 2:31) signals that the holy war starts here, east of the Jordan. Sihon's refusal and his defeat set the pattern for what follows: an offer of peace, a hardened heart, victory given by God, and the ban. Readers then and now have found that pattern troubling as well as triumphant.

views.H: Israel's route around Edom and through the edge of Moab, and the defeat of Sihon and Og, are remembered in Numbers 20–21, Judges 11:12–27 and the Psalms. Many conservative scholars hold the details, including the asides on older peoples, to be early notes, by Moses or a later scribe.
views.C: Critical scholars notice that this route differs from Numbers 20:14–21, where Edom refuses passage and Israel turns away. The friendly picture of Edom here may reflect a time before the hostility of the exile period. The giant names are read as old traditions about earlier peoples, and the account of Sihon as a model for the ideal of the holy war.
views.T: The historical prologue continues: the overlord recounts how he set boundaries and gave territories. Treaties of the time often list lands that a vassal may not touch. Here the great king protects other lands as well as giving Israel its own.
views.J: The Talmud says God told Israel to spare Moab and Ammon for the sake of two women who would come from them, Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite, mother of King Rehoboam (Bavli Bava Kamma 38b). The sages read the peace offer to Sihon (2:26) as the model for the rule that every war must begin with an offer of peace (Sifre Deuteronomy on 20:10; Rashi on 2:26).
views.X: Paul's speech in Acts 17:26 says God "determined the boundaries" where nations live, an idea close to this chapter. Christian readers have also used the respect for Edom, Moab and Ammon as an example of God's care for peoples outside Israel.

deep.b:
The word cherem, here "under the ban" (2:34; 3:6), means something set apart for God and taken out of human use, often by destruction. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription of about 840 BC, uses the same word: King Mesha says he killed the people of Nebo, because he had devoted it to his god Ashtar-Chemosh. So the practice was known among Israel's neighbors.

Readers take the commands in several ways. A traditional reading holds that God, as judge, used Israel to punish nations whose sin was "complete" (Genesis 15:16), at one moment in history, and never as a pattern for later war. Others, such as Paul Copan and Nicholas Wolterstorff, argue that the language of total destruction is a form of ancient war rhetoric, since Joshua and Judges show many of the same peoples still living in the land. Critical scholars such as Moshe Weinfeld see the ban as an ideal written in the 7th century to forbid any mixing with Canaanite religion, at a time when there were no Canaanites to fight. Others, such as Eric Seibert, think the texts show a view of God that later Scripture corrects. The chapter 7 page returns to the question.

echoes: Genesis 14:5–6; Genesis 15:16; Genesis 19:36–38; Genesis 36:1–43; Numbers 14:29–35; Numbers 20:14–21; Numbers 21:21–32; Judges 11:12–27; Psalm 135:10–12; Psalm 136:17–22; Amos 2:9; Acts 17:26

settings.what: The LORD's orders about Edom, Moab and Ammon
settings.by: The LORD, as Moses reports his words
settings.to: Israel near Mount Seir at the end of the wilderness years, recalled before all Israel on the plains of Moab
settings.when: as Israel turns north toward the land after thirty-eight years
settings.why: God forbids Israel to take land from the descendants of Esau and Lot. He gave them their lands, as he will give Israel its own. Israel must pay for food and water. For hearers about to fight for their land, the lesson is that the LORD rules all nations. The conquest is a gift with limits, not a license to take whatever they can. The asides on the old giant peoples (2:10–12, 20–23) speak past Moses' hearers to later readers, who knew these lands. The story continues in 2:24–3:11.

settings.what: Orders against Sihon and Og, and an offer of peace
settings.by: The LORD, and Moses, as Moses reports
settings.to: Israel at the Arnon; Sihon king of Heshbon, through messengers; recalled before all Israel on the plains of Moab
settings.when: as Israel moves north into the land east of the Jordan
settings.why: God hands over Sihon and later Og, and tells Moses not to fear. Moses first sends Sihon an offer of peace and asks only to pass through, paying for food and water. Sihon refuses and is defeated. For the hearers, these were the victories they had just seen (1:4). They are proof that God will do the same west of the Jordan (3:21–22). The offer of peace also matches the law of war in 20:10.

title: Og, the Eastern Tribes, and a Prayer Refused
sum: Og king of Bashan comes out to fight at Edrei, and Israel defeats him as it did Sihon, taking sixty walled towns (3:1–11). His huge iron bed, still shown at Rabbah, is the sign of a giant race. Moses gives the land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, on condition that their fighting men cross over and fight with their brothers (3:12–20). He charges Joshua not to be afraid (3:21–22). Then Moses tells of his own prayer to cross and see the good land. God refuses: "That is enough from you!" He may only look from Pisgah, and must give Joshua his charge (3:23–29).
Moses' prayer is one of the most human moments in the Torah. The man who prayed Israel through every crisis cannot win this one request for himself.
readings: Read as a pause before the end

The victories over Sihon and Og are the first fruits of the conquest, and the eastern tribes receive land at once. But the chapter ends with Moses standing outside, looking in. The book's whole setting "across from Beth-peor" (3:29) is the place where the people once sinned with the Baal of Peor (Numbers 25), a reminder that the old generation's grave is nearby.
Read as a prayer

Moses' prayer (3:24–25) begins with praise, "you have begun to let your servant see your greatness," and then asks. The rabbis counted it as the model of how to pray: praise first, request after (Bavli Berakhot 32a). They said Moses prayed 515 times, the number-value of va'etchannan, "I pleaded" (Deuteronomy Rabbah 11:10). God's answer shows that even the greatest prayer can be refused.

views.H: The asides about Og's bed (3:11) and about Jair's towns "to this day" (3:14) are read either as Moses' own notes or as short additions by a later prophet, much as the account of Moses' death was added. The defeat of Og is also recalled in Numbers 21:33–35, Psalm 135 and Psalm 136.
views.C: "To this day" suggests a writer living long after the event, when the bed could still be seen in the Ammonite capital. Some scholars connect it with a large basalt dolmen or a ritual bed like the one in the temple of Marduk in Babylon. The settling of the eastern tribes and their duty to fight is read as a theme of the Deuteronomistic History (Joshua 1:12–18; Joshua 22).
views.T: The overlord grants land to his vassals, with a condition. The eastern tribes receive their portion before the others, but their gift depends on their loyalty to the whole people.
views.J: The portion read in synagogue, Va'etchannan ("I pleaded"), begins at 3:23 and is read on the Sabbath after the Ninth of Av, the Sabbath of Comfort. The rabbis tell many legends of Moses' prayer, in which he begged to enter even as a bird or a beast, and God said, "That is enough" (Deuteronomy Rabbah 11:10; Sifre Deuteronomy 26).
views.X: Christian readers have noticed that Moses finally does stand in the land, on the mountain of the transfiguration with Jesus and Elijah (Matthew 17:1–8; Luke 9:28–36). Church fathers read Moses' exclusion as a sign that the law cannot bring people into the promised rest, while Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus, leads them in.

deep.b: The text says that Og alone "was left of the last of the Rephaim," and that his bed of iron, nine cubits long and four wide (about 13 by 6 feet), could still be seen in Rabbah of the Ammonites (3:11). The word 'eres means a bed or couch, sometimes a funeral couch. Readers have taken it in four ways: a real bed made large for display; a coffin or sarcophagus, perhaps of black basalt, which looks like iron; one of the stone dolmens, ancient tombs of large slabs that are common in the Golan and the hills of Gilead; or a ritual bed, since the Babylonian Esagila Tablet gives the bed in the shrine on top of Marduk's ziggurat, Etemenanki, as 9 by 4 cubits, the same size. Alan Millard has pointed out that iron was a prestige metal in the late Bronze Age and could be used to decorate furniture. Ugaritic texts mention the rapi'uma, honored dead kings, and a god-king who ruled at Ashtaroth and Edrei, the very towns of Og (Joshua 12:4).

echoes: Numbers 21:33–35; Numbers 32:1–42; Numbers 27:12–23; Joshua 1:12–18; Joshua 12:1–6; Joshua 13:8–33; Joshua 22:1–9; Psalm 135:11; Psalm 136:20; Amos 4:1; Matthew 17:1–8

settings.what: Moses' orders to the eastern tribes and to Joshua
settings.to: The fighting men of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, and Joshua, recalled before all Israel
settings.when: after the land east of the Jordan was given to the two and a half tribes
settings.why: The tribes who already have land must cross armed ahead of their brothers until all Israel has rest. Joshua must not fear, because the LORD fights for Israel. The words bind the eastern tribes to the whole nation, and Joshua 1:12–18 and 22:1–6 show the promise kept.

settings.what: Moses' prayer to cross, and God's refusal
settings.by: Moses (the prayer) and the LORD (the answer)
settings.to: The LORD; then retold to all Israel on the plains of Moab
settings.when: after the victories over Sihon and Og, at the edge of the land
settings.why: Moses pleads to see the good land and is refused: "That is enough from you!" (3:26). He may only look from Pisgah and must give Joshua his charge. Moses tells the people that the LORD was angry with him "because of you." By telling them, he shows the cost of the people's rebellion and hands his task to Joshua. The listeners learn that even Moses stands under the word he gives them.

title: No Form, Only a Voice
sum: Moses moves from history to its lesson. Israel must keep God's rules without adding or taking away, for they are its wisdom before the nations (4:1–8). Above all they must remember Horeb, where they heard the voice of words from the fire but saw no form, and so must make no image of any kind, and not worship sun, moon or stars (4:9–24). If they do, they will be scattered among the nations, but from there they will seek the LORD and find him (4:25–31). Nothing like the exodus and Horeb has happened anywhere: "the LORD is God... There is no other" (4:32–40). Moses sets aside three towns of refuge, and a heading introduces the law (4:41–49).
This is Deuteronomy's great sermon on what kind of God Israel serves: a God heard, not seen.
readings: Read as theology

The chapter is one of the clearest statements of monotheism in the Bible. "the LORD is God. Apart from him there is no other" (4:35), and again "in the sky above and on the earth below" (4:39). The ban on images follows from the event at Horeb: Israel met God as a voice, not a shape. Everything that can be seen, human or animal, sky or star, belongs to creation, not to God.
Read as a prophecy of exile

Moses foresees that the people will grow old in the land, make images, be scattered, and serve gods of wood and stone (4:25–28). Then "from there" they will search for God and find him (4:29–31). For readers in the exile, or after it, the chapter is a word to them: the covenant still stands, and turning back is possible.

views.H: Moses, at the end of his life, warns of what he knows the people are capable of, as Joshua and the prophets later did. The promise of return is a prophecy fulfilled when Israel came back from Babylon.
views.C: Many scholars, following Jon Levenson and others, see 4:1–40 as one of the latest parts of the book, written in the exile with its warnings and promises written after the event. Its sharp monotheism matches Isaiah 40–48 ("I am the LORD, and there is no other"). The heading in 4:44–49 is seen as the original start of an earlier book.
views.T: The chapter has the parts of a treaty in small: the great king's deeds, the main command (no other gods, no images), blessings and curses, and witnesses: "I call the heavens and the earth as witnesses against you today" (4:26). Assyrian and Hittite treaties also invoke heaven and earth.
views.J: Maimonides built on this chapter his principle that God has no body or form (Guide of the Perplexed 1:1–3; Thirteen Principles, the third). "you who held on to the LORD your God are all alive today" (4:4) is recited before the Torah reading. The rabbis took 4:9 ("Make them known to your children") as a command never to forget the day at Sinai.
views.X: Christians read 4:15–19 together with John 1:18, "No one has ever seen God," and Colossians 1:15, which calls Christ "the image of the invisible God." Christian debates about icons and images, from the 8th century to the Reformation, turned largely on this chapter. Paul's sermon in Romans 1:23 echoes its list of images.

deep.h: One God, and the gods of the nations
deep.b: Deuteronomy 4 says that "the LORD is God... There is no other" (4:35; 4:39). Yet 4:19 says that the sun, moon and stars have been "given... as a share to all the peoples," and 10:17 calls the LORD "the God of gods." Scholars take this in several ways. Some, such as Nathan MacDonald, argue that Deuteronomy is not making a philosophical claim that other gods do not exist, but a claim of loyalty: the LORD alone is Israel's God and alone is God in the full sense. Others, such as Mark Smith, see a development from an older view in which the LORD was the chief of a council of gods (compare 32:8–9) to a strict monotheism in the exile. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take 4:35 and 4:39 at face value and read "gods" elsewhere as false gods or created spirits. Richard Bauckham proposes that what sets the LORD apart in the Bible is that he alone is creator and ruler of all, a definition Christians later used to speak of Jesus.

Deuteronomy gives its reason for the ban on images from experience: "You saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the fire" (4:15). The Hebrew temunah, "form" or "shape," is used in Numbers 12:8 for what Moses saw, so the point is not that God has no presence but that Israel saw none it could copy. The list of forbidden images in 4:16–19 runs backward through the creation story of Genesis 1: humans, animals, birds, creeping things, fish, then the lights of the sky. Michael Fishbane and others have noted the reversal: Israel is not to worship any created thing. Archaeology shows that images of God were common in the region. Tryggve Mettinger has shown that early Israel may have used empty standing stones or an empty throne, the cherubim above the ark, as a way of marking God's presence without a statue.

echoes: Genesis 1:14–27; Exodus 19:16–20; Exodus 20:4–6; Exodus 20:18–22; Exodus 21:12–14; Exodus 34:6; Numbers 35:9–34; 1 Kings 8:46–53; Isaiah 40:18–26; Isaiah 45:5–22; Jeremiah 29:12–14; John 1:18; Acts 17:24–29; Romans 1:22–25; Hebrews 12:18–29

settings.what: Sermon: no form, only a voice
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: at the close of his first speech, just before the law is set out
settings.why: Moses draws the lesson of the history. Israel heard the LORD's voice at Horeb but saw no form, so it must make no image and worship nothing in the sky. The law is Israel's wisdom before the nations, and nothing may be added or taken away. If later generations make idols, they will be scattered among the nations, but from there they will seek the LORD and find him (4:25–31). The sermon gives the reason for the whole book: "the LORD is God in the sky above and on the earth below. There is no other" (4:39).
views: Traditional readers hear Moses foreseeing what would happen if Israel turned to idols.

Many critical scholars date the chapter to the exile, because it speaks so clearly of scattering and return and of the LORD as the only God. For exiles surrounded by Babylon's images, it says that their God is not lost with the land and can be found where they are.

settings.what: A law put into effect: three towns of refuge east of the Jordan
settings.by: Moses (an act, told by the narrator; no one speaks)
settings.to: The eastern tribes, and anyone who kills by accident in their land
settings.when: after the first speech, before the law is set out
settings.why: Moses sets apart Bezer, Ramoth and Golan for anyone who kills a neighbor by accident. The law protects the one who kills without hatred from the avenger of blood. It applies in the land already won, and it shows the new generation that the law begins to work at once. The full law comes in 19:1–13.

traditions.q: Israel saw no form at Horeb (4:15). May Christians make and honor images of Christ and the saints?
views: Yes. God had no visible form before, but in Christ the invisible God became visible, so he may be painted (John of Damascus). The Second Council of Nicaea (787) taught that icons are venerated, honored with a kiss or a candle, while worship belongs to God alone, and the Orthodox celebrate this every year on the Sunday of Orthodoxy.
Yes. The Incarnation began a new order of images, and the honor given to an image passes to the person it shows (Catechism 2129–2132). Catholics use statues as well as paintings.

Images may stay in churches as reminders and for teaching, as long as no one worships them. Luther opposed the smashing of images by Karlstadt and counted the ban on images as part of the first commandment.

No image of God may be made, and images of Christ may not be used in worship, because God wants his people taught by the living preaching of his word (Heidelberg Catechism Q96–98). Calvin built his case largely on this chapter (Institutes 1.11), and Reformed churches removed images.

title: The Ten Words Again
sum: Moses calls all Israel together: the LORD did not make the covenant at Horeb with their ancestors: "He made it with us, we who are here today, all of us alive" (5:3). He repeats the Ten Words, close to Exodus 20 but with changes, above all in the Sabbath command, which now looks back to slavery in Egypt (5:6–21). Then he recalls how the people, terrified by the fire, asked him to hear God for them. God agreed, wishing they would always have such a heart, and kept Moses on the mountain to receive the rest of the command (5:22–33).
The chapter is the foundation of everything that follows. The laws of chapters 12–26 are presented as the explanation of these Ten Words, which God spoke to all and "added nothing more" (5:22).
readings: Read as a covenant renewed

The generation that heard the Ten Words at Horeb is dead (2:14–16). Yet Moses says the covenant was made "with us." Each new generation is to receive the covenant as if it had stood at the mountain, as Jews still say at Passover that each person should see himself as if he came out of Egypt.
Read beside Exodus 20

The two forms of the Ten Words differ in about twenty small details. Placed side by side, they show how the same commands could be explained for new hearers. Sabbath rest is grounded in creation in Exodus and in the exodus here. The neighbor's wife is put first in the last command here, and the field is added. The notes and the section below set out the differences and how they have been explained.

views.H: Moses quotes the Ten Words from memory, adding explanations, since a preacher repeating a text adds his own emphasis. The tablets themselves held the words as God spoke them. The rabbis say both forms were spoken at once, in a single word (Bavli Shevuot 20b), something no human mouth could do.
views.C: Most scholars think the Deuteronomy form is later than the Exodus form in some places and earlier in others. The Sabbath reason and the order of wife and house in 5:21 are often taken as Deuteronomy's revisions for a society that cared about the place of women and the memory of slavery. Some think both forms grew from a shorter set of ten commands.
views.T: The Ten Words are the basic terms of the treaty, spoken by the great king himself and written on two tablets, like treaty copies kept in the sanctuaries of both parties. Meredith Kline argued that the two tablets were two copies of the whole covenant, one for God and one for Israel.
views.J: Jewish tradition counts the Ten Words differently from most Christians: "I am the LORD your God" (5:6) is the first saying, and the ban on other gods and images is the second. The sages refused to let the Ten Words be recited daily in the synagogue, so that no one could say only these were given at Sinai (Bavli Berakhot 12a). Both forms are read publicly in the yearly cycle.
views.X: Jesus cites the commands about murder, adultery, stealing, false witness and honoring parents in his answer to the rich man (Mark 10:19), and Paul sums up the commands about the neighbor in "love your neighbor" (Romans 13:8–10). Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, count the last verse as two commands (wife, and property), while Reformed and Orthodox churches count the ban on images as a separate command. Deuteronomy's division of 5:21 lies behind Augustine's count.

deep.h: Two forms of the Ten Words
deep.b:
Placed beside Exodus 20:2–17, Deuteronomy's form has these main differences:

  • Sabbath. Exodus says "Remember the day of the Sabbath" (Exodus 20:8); Deuteronomy says "Keep" (5:12). Deuteronomy adds the ox and the donkey to the list of those who rest, and the purpose clause "Then your slave, man or woman, can rest just as you do" (5:14). Its reason is the exodus, "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (5:15), where Exodus gives creation (Exodus 20:11).
  • Parents. Deuteronomy adds "as the LORD your God commanded you" and the promise "so that it will go well with you" (5:16).
  • The commands about the neighbor are joined by "and" in Deuteronomy (5:18–21), making them one list.
  • Witness. Exodus says "a lying witness"; Deuteronomy, 'ed shav', "an empty witness" (5:20), a wider word for worthless or deceitful speech.
  • Craving. Exodus puts the house first, then the wife; Deuteronomy puts the wife first, then the house, and adds "his field." It uses two verbs: "crave" for the wife, "long for" for property (5:21).

Jewish tradition says God spoke "remember" and "keep" at the same moment (Bavli Shevuot 20b), and the Friday-night hymn Lekhah Dodi sings, "Keep and remember, in a single word." Traditional Christian scholars usually say Moses, preaching, explained the text he had received. Critical scholars see a deliberate revision: Deuteronomy's writers made the Sabbath a law of social justice and treated a wife as more than property. Either way, the differences show that from the start the commands were explained and applied.

The Hebrew velo yasaf in 5:22 most likely means "he did not add," so the Ten Words alone were spoken by God to all the people, and everything else came through Moses. That is the reading of Rashbam, Ibn Ezra and most modern versions. Targum Onkelos and Rashi read it differently, as "he did not stop": God's voice went on without ceasing, a voice that still speaks. The difference matters to how the law is understood. One reading sets the Ten Words apart as unique; the other makes all later teaching part of one ongoing word from Sinai.

echoes: Exodus 19:16–25; Exodus 20:1–21; Exodus 24:12; Exodus 31:18; Exodus 34:1–28; Leviticus 19:3–4; Psalm 81:9–10; Jeremiah 7:9; Hosea 4:2; Matthew 5:21–30; Matthew 19:17–19; Mark 10:19; Romans 7:7; Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2–3; James 2:10–11

settings.what: Moses' second speech: the covenant and its laws
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: the main speech of the book, introduced by the heading in 4:44–49
settings.why: This is the heart of the book. Moses first repeats the Ten Words and the people's request at Horeb (5). Then he preaches on loving the LORD and remembering him in a rich land (6–11). Then he sets out the laws for life in the land (12–26). He ends with the blessings and curses (28). The ceremony of chapter 27 breaks in. Moses insists that the covenant was made "with us, we who are here today, all of us alive" (5:3). Every later reader is meant to stand in that crowd.
views: Many scholars note that the speech follows the order of an ancient treaty: history, stipulations, a written copy, witnesses, blessings and curses. Kline and Kitchen compare it to Hittite treaties of about 1400–1200 BC. Weinfeld and others compare it to Assyrian loyalty oaths of the 7th century BC.
Most critical scholars think this speech, without the frame, is close to the scroll that King Josiah heard read in 622 BC (2 Kings 22:8–13).

settings.what: The Ten Words
settings.by: The LORD, as Moses repeats his words
settings.to: All Israel at Horeb, who heard God's voice from the fire; repeated to their children on the plains of Moab
settings.why: The Ten Words bind every Israelite, man and woman, slave and free. The Sabbath rest reaches even the foreigner and the animals. They are close to Exodus 20:2–17, with changes. Above all, the Sabbath command now looks back to slavery in Egypt, so that slaves too may rest (5:15). And the neighbor's wife is set apart from his house and goods. Spoken again to the new generation, the Words become the summary that the laws of chapters 12–26 explain.

settings.what: The people's request: Moses must hear for them
settings.by: Moses, recalling the elders' words and the LORD's reply
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: remembering the day at Horeb when the people heard the voice from the fire
settings.why: The tribal heads and elders were afraid of dying. They asked Moses to go near and hear God for them. God approved, and kept Moses on the mountain to receive the rest of the command. The story tells the hearers why the laws come through Moses and not straight from God's voice. It also prepares for the promise of a prophet like Moses in 18:15–18.

traditions.q: How are the Ten Commandments numbered?
views: Following Augustine, the ban on other gods and on images is one commandment, and the ban on craving is split in two, following this chapter: the neighbor's wife (ninth) and the neighbor's goods (tenth) (Catechism 2066). Making images is read as part of the ban on other gods.
Lutherans use Augustine's count like Catholics, but Luther's catechisms follow the order of Exodus 20:17, so the ninth is the neighbor's house and the tenth his wife and everything else.

The ban on images is the second commandment and the ban on craving is one, following the ancient count of Philo, Josephus and Origen (Heidelberg Catechism Q92). Reformed churches held that the Catholic count hid the image ban.
The Orthodox use the same count as the Reformed, the oldest Christian count, yet they venerate icons, reading the second commandment as a ban on idols rather than on all religious images.
Anglicans use the same count as the Reformed and Orthodox, and the Book of Common Prayer had the Ten Commandments read aloud at the start of the Communion service.

title: Listen, Israel
sum: Moses gives the command in its shortest form. "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one. Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (6:4–5). The words are to be on the heart, repeated to children, spoken at home and on the road, bound on hand and forehead and written on doorposts (6:6–9). In the good land, full of houses and vineyards they did not make, they must not forget the LORD or test him as at Massah (6:10–19). When a child asks what the laws mean, the answer is the story of the exodus (6:20–25).
The Shema is the creed of Judaism and, through Jesus, the first commandment of Christianity.
readings: Read as a creed

The first line is a confession: the LORD, and no other, is Israel's God, and he is one. Jews say it every morning and evening, and at the moment of death. Its grammar is open to several readings (see the note on 6:4), but every reading joins two claims: loyalty to the LORD alone, and the unity of God.
Read as a way of life

The Shema is not only a belief but a practice. Love is commanded, and it reaches the whole person, the heart, the being and the strength. It is taught to children, spoken at every time of day, worn on the body and fixed to the house. Love here is like the loyalty a vassal owes a great king: shown in obedience, not only in feeling.

views.H: Moses gives Israel its summary of the law on the plains of Moab. Jewish and Christian tradition both take the Shema as part of Moses' last teaching, and its practices (tefillin, mezuzah) as commands to be kept as written.
views.C: Many scholars read 6:4 as a 7th-century slogan of King Josiah's reform: one God, worshiped at one place (see chapter 12). It answers a world in which the LORD could be honored in many local forms. Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud mention "YHWH of Samaria" and "YHWH of Teman," so "the LORD is one" may first have meant one LORD, not many local LORDs.
views.T: William Moran showed that "love" in Assyrian treaties means loyal obedience to the king. The treaty of Esarhaddon (672 BC) commands vassals to love the crown prince "as yourselves," to tell their children, and to keep the oath "with all your heart." The Shema takes the language of political loyalty and applies it to God.
views.J: Every morning and evening Jews recite 6:4–9, 11:13–21 and Numbers 15:37–41, with blessings before and after. The first line is said with the eyes covered, and the response "Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever" is whispered. Tefillin and the mezuzah carry these passages. Rabbi Akiva died saying the Shema, stretching out the word "one" (Bavli Berakhot 61b).
views.X: Jesus names 6:4–5 as the first commandment, adding "with all your mind," and pairs it with "love your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:18) (Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 22:34–40). Paul reworks the Shema in 1 Corinthians 8:6: "one God, the Father... and one Lord, Jesus Christ." Church fathers used the verse against the belief in many gods, and later in debates over the Trinity.

deep.b:
The Hebrew of 6:4 has six words: shema' yisra'el YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad, "Hear, Israel, the LORD our God the LORD one." It has no verb "is," and can be divided in four main ways:

  • "The LORD is our God, the LORD alone" (NJPS, NRSV). Israel worships the LORD only. This fits the sense of loyalty in the next verse and is supported by Zechariah 14:9 and by the Talmud's reading.
  • "The LORD our God is one LORD" (KJV). A claim about God's unity.
  • "The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (ESV and others). The same claim, with "the LORD our God" as the subject.
  • "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one," the reading on this site. It keeps both halves: the LORD is Israel's God, and he is one, not many.

Rashi joins the claims: the LORD who is "our God" now will be confessed by all nations as "one" in the future (Zechariah 14:9). Maimonides read "one" as absolute unity and made it a principle of faith. Christian theologians from the 4th century on noted that echad can describe a unity made of parts, as when man and wife become "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), and argued the Shema is compatible with the Trinity. Jewish thinkers reject that reading.

The Hebrew is written in Torah scrolls with two enlarged letters: the last letter of shema' ('ayin) and of echad (dalet). Together they spell 'ed, "witness." Saying the Shema is a public witness to God.

The three words of 6:5 are often read as parts of a person, but in Hebrew they build up. The heart, levav, is the inner self, including thought and will, not only feeling. The nefesh, here "being," is the whole living person and his life itself; this site avoids "soul" because it suggests a part separate from the body. The me'od, "strength," is literally "very much": all that one has. The rabbis read these as "with both your inclinations, good and bad; even if he takes your life; and with all your money" (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). The Greek translators made the list fit Greek ideas, using "mind" or "heart" for levav, and the Gospels have four terms. See the variant at 6:5.

echoes: Exodus 13:8–16; Exodus 17:1–7; Leviticus 19:18; Numbers 15:37–41; Joshua 22:5; 2 Kings 23:25; Zechariah 14:9; Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 4:7; Matthew 22:34–40; Luke 10:25–28; John 10:30; Romans 3:30; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; James 2:19

settings.what: The Shema: Listen, Israel
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: The command in its shortest form: the LORD is one, and Israel is to love him with all its heart, being and strength. The words bind every Israelite and every household. Parents must repeat them to their children, at home and on the road. They must bind them on hand and forehead and write them on doorposts and gates. Jews still say these words every morning and evening, and Jesus called them the first command (Mark 12:29–30). Spoken on the eve of entering the land, they put loyalty to the LORD at the center of daily life.
views: Many read 6:4 as a confession that the LORD is the only God.
Others, such as Block and MacDonald, read it as a call to loyalty: the LORD alone is Israel's God, whatever other powers there may be. This fits the warnings against other gods that follow.

settings.what: Warning: do not forget in a full land
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: Israel is about to receive houses, wells, vineyards and olive groves it did not make. The danger is that, full and safe, it will forget the LORD who brought it out of Egypt. Or it will test him as it did at Massah. For a people who had lived on manna, the warning looks ahead to a time of plenty.

settings.what: The answer to a child's question
settings.to: Israelite parents, heads of households in the land, and through them their children
settings.when: when a child asks what the laws mean
settings.why: The answer to "why?" is a story: we were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD brought us out. The laws are for our good. This makes every household a school, and it ties each law to the memory of the exodus. The Passover Haggadah takes up this question and answer.

traditions.q: The LORD is one (6:4). Does the Shema leave room for the Trinity?
views: Yes. There is only one God, one in being, and in that one God there are three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Catechism 200–202, 253). Jesus himself repeats the Shema (Mark 12:29), and Paul places him inside it (1 Corinthians 8:6).

Yes. The one God is the Father, from whom the Son is eternally born and the Spirit eternally comes, so the three share one nature. The Orthodox reject the Western addition to the Nicene Creed that the Spirit comes from the Father and the Son.

Pentecostals are divided. Trinitarian Pentecostals, such as the Assemblies of God, hold the historic doctrine; Oneness Pentecostals, such as the United Pentecostal Church International, read the Shema as one God who shows himself as Father, Son and Spirit, and baptize in the name of Jesus alone.
The Shema means that Jehovah alone is God. Jesus is God's Son and his first creation, not equal to the Father, and the holy spirit is God's active force, not a person.

The Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings, and the Father and Son have glorified bodies (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22). They are one in purpose, will and love, which is how Latter-day Saints read the oneness of the Shema.

title: A Treasured People
sum: When God brings Israel into the land and hands over the seven nations, Israel must put them under the ban, make no covenant or marriage with them, and destroy their altars, standing stones and Asherah poles (7:1–5). The reason is Israel's calling: it is a holy people, God's "own private treasure," chosen not for its size but because God loved it and kept his oath (7:6–11). Obedience will bring blessing on children, herds and crops, and freedom from disease (7:12–16). Israel must not fear the nations; God will clear them out bit by bit, and their idols must be burned (7:17–26).
The chapter puts two of the Bible's hardest ideas side by side: the commands to destroy, and God's free choice of a small people out of love.
readings: Read as a call to holiness

On this reading the center of the chapter is not war but worship. The danger of the Canaanites is their gods: "they will turn your sons away from following me" (7:4). Marriage, treaties and idols are banned because they would draw Israel into other worship. That is why the same chapter that commands the ban spends most of its words on God's love and Israel's loyalty.
Read as a command to destroy

Others read the opening verses at face value as an order to wipe out whole peoples, and find it hard to fit with the God who "loves the foreigner" (10:18). Readers have answered in many ways: by limiting the command to one time and place, by reading it as hyperbole, by treating it as a judgment on those nations' sins, or by saying that later Scripture corrects it. The section below sets out the main views.

views.H: God commanded Israel to drive out the nations of Canaan in judgment on their sins (9:4–5; Genesis 15:16), for that generation only. The command was not carried out completely, as Joshua and Judges show, and later Israel failed through the very mixing this chapter warns against.
views.C: Most critical scholars read the chapter as 7th-century writing, when the Canaanite nations had long disappeared. Its ban is a theological way of saying: have nothing to do with other worship. The list of seven nations is a fixed formula, and the warnings against marriage reflect later concerns, as in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13.
views.T: Treaties demanded that vassals have no dealings with the great king's enemies, and Assyrian treaties forbade any treaty with other kings. The blessings of 7:12–16 are like the blessings promised to a loyal vassal.
views.J: The rabbis counted the command not to marry Canaanites as a law with limits: they applied it only to the seven nations, not to converts or to other peoples (Bavli Avodah Zarah 36b). Maimonides ruled that the seven nations no longer exist, so the command to destroy them is no longer in force (Mishneh Torah, Kings 5:4). The words "own private treasure" and "chosen" are read as the source of Israel's special calling, not of superiority (7:7).
views.X: 1 Peter 2:9 calls the church "a chosen people... a holy nation, a people for God's own possession," words from this chapter and Exodus 19:5–6. Christian theologians from Origen on have read the war against the nations as a picture of the struggle against sin, while debating the literal sense.

deep.b:
The command "put them under the ban completely... and do not show them mercy" (7:2) is one of the most troubling in Scripture. The main ways of reading it:

  • A unique judgment. God, the judge of all nations, used Israel once to punish peoples whose sin had reached its limit (9:4–5; Genesis 15:16). The command was for that moment only, never to be copied. This is the traditional view of many Jews and Christians.
  • War rhetoric. Ancient kings often boasted of total destruction when they had won only a battle. In the same chapter Moses forbids marriage with these nations (7:3), and says they will be cleared out "bit by bit" (7:22). Paul Copan and others argue the language was not meant literally.
  • A religious ideal. Many scholars think the chapter was written when no Canaanites were left, so that it really commands Israel to root out idolatry in itself. Moshe Weinfeld and Susan Niditch have shown how the ban was used as an ideology.
  • A view to be outgrown. Eric Seibert and others think the texts reflect Israel's understanding of God at the time, which the prophets and Jesus moved beyond.

Jewish law limited the command to the seven nations long gone; Christian tradition mostly read it as a picture of spiritual warfare. Every reading has to weigh the chapter's own emphasis on God's love for those he chooses and, in 10:18, for the foreigner.

Moses denies the obvious reasons for Israel's election. It was not numbers: "you were the fewest of all the peoples" (7:7). Two chapters later it is not righteousness either (9:4–6). What is left is love and promise: "It was because the LORD loved you, and because he kept the oath he swore to your ancestors" (7:8). The verb chashaq, "set his heart on," is used of a man's desire for a woman (Genesis 34:8). Jon Levenson describes this as the love of a father for a chosen son, which brings both privilege and suffering. The Bible connects Israel's choice to the blessing of all nations (Genesis 12:3), and Paul says the choice has not been withdrawn: "the gifts and calling of God cannot be taken back" (Romans 11:29, a translation made for this note).

echoes: Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis 15:16–21; Exodus 19:5–6; Exodus 23:23–33; Exodus 34:6–7; Exodus 34:11–16; Joshua 23:12–13; Judges 2:1–3; 1 Kings 11:1–8; Ezra 9:1–2; Amos 3:2; Romans 11:28–29; 1 Peter 2:9

settings.what: No covenant with the nations of the land
settings.to: Israel's army and every household, once Israel enters the land of the seven nations west of the Jordan
settings.when: on the eve of the conquest
settings.why: Israel must put the seven nations under the ban and make no treaty or marriage with them. It must destroy their altars, standing stones and Asherah poles. The problem the law answers is the pull of other gods through marriage and shared worship. The reason given is Israel's calling: it is holy to the LORD, chosen not because it was big but because God loved it (7:6–7). The commands are among the hardest in the Bible for later readers.
views: Traditional readers take the ban as a real order, limited to the nations of Canaan at that time and tied to their wickedness (9:4–5).
Some, such as Copan and Flannagan, read it as the stock overstatement of ancient war reports. They note that the same chapter forbids marrying the very people it says to destroy.

Many critical scholars point out that by the 7th century BC the Canaanite nations were long gone. For readers in Josiah's Judah, the ban was a call to tear down idols and shrines in their own land, as 2 Kings 23 tells.

title: Not by Bread Alone
sum: Moses asks Israel to remember the forty years as a time of training. God humbled them with hunger and fed them with manna, to teach them that people live "by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth" (8:1–6). Their clothes did not wear out; their feet did not swell. Now he is bringing them into a good land of streams and springs, wheat, vines and olives, iron and copper (8:7–10). There the danger is not hunger but pride: full houses, growing herds and the thought, "My own strength... won me this wealth" (8:11–17). They must remember that God gives the strength to gain wealth, or they will perish like the nations (8:18–20).
The chapter is a short teaching on two dangers: the hunger that tempts people to doubt, and the plenty that tempts them to forget.
readings: Read as a lesson in memory

The key word is "remember," with its opposite, "forget" (8:2, 8:11, 8:14, 8:18, 8:19). The wilderness, which looked like punishment, was a classroom. The land, which looks like reward, is a test. Memory is the guard against pride.
Read through Jesus' temptations

In the wilderness Jesus is hungry for forty days, and the devil tells him to make bread from stones. He answers with 8:3 (Matthew 4:4; Luke 4:4). Jesus relives Israel's test and passes it. His three answers to the devil all come from Deuteronomy 6–8 (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), so Christian readers have long read these chapters as the background of the temptation story.

views.H: Moses speaks to a generation that ate manna all its life and is about to eat the produce of the land. The manna ceases after the crossing of the Jordan, as Joshua 5:12 records.
views.C: Scholars note that the chapter is shaped as a ring, with the warnings against forgetting at the center (8:11). The picture of the land, with its iron and copper, fits the mining regions known to later Judah. The verses are read as a sermon for people already living in plenty under the monarchy.
views.T: The vassal is reminded that his wealth is the overlord's gift. To claim it as one's own achievement is to deny the treaty.
views.J: The grace after meals, Birkat ha-Mazon, comes from 8:10, and the rabbis counted it as a Torah command. The seven species of 8:8 shape Jewish blessings and the festival of first fruits. Rashi says the clouds of glory washed the people's clothes, and that the clothes grew with the children.
views.X: Jesus' answer to the devil (Matthew 4:4) and his teaching on the bread of life (John 6:31–35) draw on this chapter. Hebrews 12:5–11 develops the idea of God's discipline as a father's (8:5). Christians, too, give thanks at meals in the spirit of 8:10.

echoes: Exodus 16:1–36; Numbers 11:4–9; Numbers 21:4–9; Joshua 5:12; Nehemiah 9:20–21; Psalm 78:18–25; Proverbs 30:8–9; Hosea 13:4–6; Matthew 4:1–4; Luke 4:1–4; Luke 12:16–21; John 6:31–35; 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 10:1–5; Hebrews 12:5–11

settings.what: Sermon: not by bread alone
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: Moses explains the forty years as a time of training. God let them hunger and fed them manna to teach them that people live by every word from the LORD's mouth. In the good land the danger will be pride: "My own strength and the power of my hand have won me this wealth" (8:17). The sermon speaks to a people about to move from want to plenty. Jesus answers the devil with 8:3 (Matthew 4:4).

title: Not Because You Are Righteous
sum: Israel will cross the Jordan and defeat nations greater than itself, the Anakim among them (9:1–3). But they must not say it is because of their righteousness. It is because the nations are wicked and because God keeps his oath; Israel itself is "a stiff-necked people" (9:4–6). To prove it Moses tells the story of the golden calf. While he was on the mountain receiving the tablets, the people made an idol. He smashed the tablets, ground the calf to dust, and lay before God forty days and nights, praying for them and for Aaron (9:7–21). He lists other rebellions, at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah and Kadesh, and gives his prayer: remember Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and what Egypt would say (9:22–29).
Deuteronomy removes the ground for pride. The gift of the land rests on God's faithfulness, not Israel's.
readings: Read as a sermon against self-righteousness

Moses expects that victory will make Israel proud, and that they will read their success as a reward. He answers three times, "not because you are righteous" (9:4–6), and then tells their history of rebellion. The point is grace: the land is a gift given to the undeserving.
Read as a story of intercession

The center of the chapter is Moses on his face. God says, "Let go of me, so I can destroy them" (9:14), and Moses does not let go. The prayer of 9:26–29 appeals to God's own name, his oath and his reputation, not to Israel's merit. Many readers see in it the deepest model of prayer for others in the Old Testament.

views.H: Moses retells the calf story from his own point of view. He arranges it as a sermon, not a timeline, so the forty days of prayer are mentioned out of order (9:18, 9:25; 10:10). Traditional readers count the periods differently: Rashi counts three periods of forty days, ending on the Day of Atonement.
views.C: The account draws on the story in Exodus 32–34 but tells it differently: Moses' prayer comes later, Aaron's role is stressed, and the calf is ground and thrown into a stream. Many scholars read the calf story in both books as a polemic against the calves of Jeroboam at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30).
views.T: The story of the calf is the treaty broken. The smashed tablets are like a broken treaty document, and the new tablets (10:1–5) are the treaty renewed. Treaties often contain a section recalling past rebellions and the overlord's mercy.
views.J: The rabbis say the calf is a sin that every generation pays a little of (Bavli Sanhedrin 102a). Rashi counts the forty days: Moses went up on the seventh of Sivan, broke the tablets on the seventeenth of Tammuz, prayed forty days, and came down with the second tablets on the tenth of Tishri, the Day of Atonement. The fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz remembers the broken tablets (Mishnah Ta'anit 4:6).
views.X: Paul's teaching that salvation is not by works so that "no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8–9) has often been compared with 9:4–6. Moses' readiness to stand between God and the people is seen as a picture of Christ's intercession (Hebrews 7:25). Stephen's speech recalls the calf (Acts 7:39–41).

deep.h: Two accounts of the golden calf
deep.b:
Exodus 32–34 and Deuteronomy 9:7–10:11 tell the same story with different emphasis. In Exodus, God tells Moses of the calf and Moses prays at once on the mountain (Exodus 32:7–14), then comes down, breaks the tablets, burns the calf and makes the people drink the water (Exodus 32:19–20). In Deuteronomy, Moses goes down at once, and his prayers come after the tablets are broken (9:18–20; 9:25–29). Deuteronomy adds that God was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him (9:20). It also leaves out the Levites' slaughter of the people and the drinking of the water. Exodus mentions God's name as merciful and slow to anger (Exodus 34:6–7); Deuteronomy, which never quotes that formula in this story, puts its weight on Moses' prayer.

Traditional readers harmonize the accounts, taking Deuteronomy as Moses' summary. Critical scholars often see Deuteronomy as a later retelling that adjusts the Exodus story, or as drawing on an older form of it. Both note that Deuteronomy uses the story as proof of its main point: Israel did not earn the land.

deep.title: Claude's reading: the forty days as a frame
deep.b: My own suggestion about the repeated forty days in 9:9, 9:11, 9:18, 9:25 and 10:10. The repetition is not only confused chronology. Moses frames the whole story of the calf with time spent before God: forty days receiving the tablets, forty days on his face, forty days receiving them again. Inside the frame stand Israel's sins. The shape says that the people's failure is held, on every side, by a mediator's time with God. This reading does not decide whether the periods were one, two or three. It explains why the speech keeps going back to the number: the forty days are the covenant's lifeline, in the same way the forty years in the wilderness were its school (8:2).

echoes: Exodus 17:1–7; Exodus 24:12–18; Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:1–35; Exodus 34:1–9; Numbers 11:1–3; Numbers 11:31–34; Numbers 14:11–19; 1 Kings 12:28–30; Psalm 106:19–23; Ezekiel 36:22–32; Acts 7:39–41; Romans 9:15–16; Ephesians 2:8–9; Hebrews 7:25

settings.what: Sermon: not because you are righteous
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: Moses takes away any ground for pride before the conquest. Israel will win, but not because it is righteous. It will win because the nations are wicked and the LORD keeps his oath to the ancestors. As proof he tells of the golden calf and other rebellions, and of his own forty days of prayer for them. The new generation hears that the land is a gift of mercy to a stubborn people.

settings.what: Moses' prayer for Israel after the golden calf
settings.to: The LORD; retold to all Israel on the plains of Moab
settings.when: at Horeb, during forty days and nights on his face before God
settings.why: Moses asks God not to destroy his people. He appeals to God's promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and to God's name among the nations. He does not appeal to any goodness in Israel. Retold to the new generation, the prayer shows them why they are alive at all.

title: New Tablets and a Circumcised Heart
sum: God tells Moses to cut two new tablets and make an ark of acacia wood. God writes the Ten Words again, and Moses puts the tablets in the ark (10:1–5). An aside records Aaron's death and the choosing of the tribe of Levi to carry the ark, serve and bless; the LORD is its inheritance (10:6–9). Then Moses asks, "what is the LORD your God asking from you?" To fear, walk, love and serve him (10:12–13). The God who owns the heavens chose Israel's ancestors. So they must circumcise their hearts, for this God shows no favoritism, defends the orphan and widow, and loves the foreigner, as Israel must too (10:14–22).
The chapter turns from the broken covenant to its renewal, and from the stone tablets to the heart.
readings: Read as a covenant restored

After the calf, everything is given again: new tablets in God's writing, a box to keep them, a tribe to carry them, and permission to go on (10:11). The ark becomes the sign that the covenant has survived Israel's sin.
Read as a summary of the law

Verses 12–22 are one of the great summaries of the whole Torah, close to Micah 6:8. They join love of God and love of neighbor: the God who is "the God of gods and the Lord of lords" (10:17) is the defender of the weakest, and his people must love the foreigner because they were foreigners in Egypt (10:19).

views.H: Moses continues the story of Horeb, adding the ark and the new tablets. The aside of 10:6–9 is read either as Moses' own note or as a later scribe's, recording events of the fortieth year.
views.C: Critical scholars see in 10:1–5 Deuteronomy's own account of the ark as a simple box for the tablets, without the gold and the cherubim of Exodus 25 and 37. The travel notes of 10:6–7 differ from Numbers 33:31–38 and are often taken as a fragment of an old itinerary inserted later.
views.T: The new tablets are the renewed treaty document, deposited in the sanctuary as treaties were kept before the gods. The call to "fear... walk... love... serve" uses the vocabulary of loyalty owed to a king.
views.J: The rabbis read 10:12 as "What does the LORD ask of you, but to fear him," and said, "Everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven" (Bavli Berakhot 33b). They taught that both the broken and the whole tablets were kept in the ark (Bavli Berakhot 8b), and drew from it a lesson to honor an old scholar who has forgotten his learning. The command to love the foreigner (10:19) is the basis for the treatment of converts.
views.X: Paul's "circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit" (Romans 2:29) draws on 10:16 and Jeremiah 4:4. Revelation 17:14 and 19:16 give Christ the title "Lord of lords and King of kings," an echo of 10:17. James 1:27 joins worship with care for orphans and widows.

deep.b: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart" (10:16) is a bold image. Physical circumcision, the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10–14), marks the body; here the command reaches inward. A "foreskinned" or uncircumcised heart is one closed or unresponsive, as an uncircumcised ear cannot hear (Jeremiah 6:10). The same idea appears in Leviticus 26:41 and Jeremiah 4:4. Later in Deuteronomy God promises to do this himself (see 30:6). Jewish tradition never treated the image as replacing the physical rite. Philo held both together. Paul says, "circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (Romans 2:29, a translation made for this note), and the Dead Sea Scrolls also speak of circumcising "the foreskin of the inclination" (Community Rule 5:5).

echoes: Exodus 25:10–22; Exodus 34:1–4; Exodus 37:1–9; Numbers 3:5–10; Numbers 18:20–24; Numbers 20:22–29; Numbers 33:31–38; 1 Kings 8:9; Jeremiah 4:4; Micah 6:8; Psalm 136:2–3; Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 2:28–29; James 1:27; Revelation 19:16

settings.what: Sermon: what the LORD asks of you
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: Moses sums up the covenant: fear the LORD, walk in his ways, love him and serve him with all the heart (10:12). The God who owns the heavens defends the orphan and widow and loves the foreigner. So Israel must love the foreigner too, "for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (10:19). The land drinks rain from the sky. So Israel's life there depends on God's care and on its faithfulness (11:10–17). These words bind every Israelite and every household (11:18–21).

title: Rain from the Sky, Blessing and Curse
sum: Moses calls the people to love God and keep his command, because they themselves saw his great deeds: the plagues of Egypt, the sea, the wilderness, and the earth opening under Dathan and Abiram (11:1–9). The land they are entering is not like Egypt, watered by the Nile and the foot; it drinks the rain of the sky, and God's eyes are always on it (11:10–12). If they obey, God will send the rain at its time; if they serve other gods, the sky will close (11:13–17). They must put these words on their hearts, hands, children and doors (11:18–25). Then Moses sets before them a blessing and a curse, to be proclaimed on Mounts Gerizim and Ebal (11:26–32).
The chapter closes the long opening of Deuteronomy and opens the laws. Everything that follows is a choice between two roads.
readings: Read as a teaching about the land

Egypt has a river; Canaan has rain. In a land watered from the sky, the harvest depends on God's care every year. The geography itself teaches dependence. The passage 11:13–21 joins this to the Shema, so that each day's prayer recalls that rain and food are covenant gifts.
Read as a choice

The final verses put the whole book into one choice: blessing or curse (11:26–28). The two mountains near Shechem, one green and one bare, as later travelers liked to say, will stand as the visible sign of the choice. Deuteronomy ends its sermon the same way, with life and death set before the people (see 30:15–20).

views.H: Moses addresses the people who saw the events of the exodus as children and young people, and commands a ceremony to be held when they arrive, which Joshua carries out (Joshua 8:30–35).
views.C: Critical scholars see 11:26–32 as a link to the ceremony of chapter 27, which places Israel's covenant at Shechem, perhaps reflecting an old northern tradition. The Samaritans later built their temple on Mount Gerizim and read the passage as naming it the chosen place.
views.T: The blessings and curses are the sanctions of the treaty, and the ceremony on the mountains is the oath-taking. In Assyrian treaties as well, rain and harvest depend on loyalty, and drought is a curse.
views.J: 11:13–21 is the second paragraph of the daily Shema, recited morning and evening; the rabbis called it "accepting the yoke of the commands" after the first paragraph's "yoke of the kingdom of heaven" (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). Its words are written in tefillin and the mezuzah. The plural "your" of this section, against the singular of the first, was read as the community's reward and punishment.
views.X: Christian readers have compared the rain promised for obedience with Jesus' word that God sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and with James 5:7, which speaks of the early and late rains. The two ways of blessing and curse are echoed in Jesus' parable of the two houses (Matthew 7:24–27).

echoes: Exodus 14:21–31; Numbers 16:1–35; Leviticus 26:3–20; Joshua 1:3–4; Joshua 8:30–35; 1 Kings 8:35–36; 1 Kings 17:1; Jeremiah 5:24; Joel 2:23; Matthew 5:45; Matthew 7:24–27; James 5:7; John 4:20

settings.what: A blessing and a curse set before Israel
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: at the close of the opening sermons, just before the laws
settings.why: Moses puts two roads before the people. He orders a ceremony at Mounts Gerizim and Ebal near Shechem, once they have crossed the Jordan. It makes the laws that follow a choice with life or death in it. The ceremony is carried out in 27:11–26 and Joshua 8:30–35.
views: Many scholars think the Shechem ceremony keeps an old northern covenant tradition, much older than the book's final form.
